newsitem.title: JAPAN: Stocks and yen seen as medium-term threats to JGBs.
newsitem.headline: Stocks and yen seen as medium-term threats to JGBs.

text.p: Japanese government bonds (JGBs) may have more room to rebound after their recent sharp fall, but stronger stock prices and the yen's weakness remain as medium-term threats, analysts and strategists said on Thursday.

"JGBs may continue to rise for a few more days before going down again. The benchmark futures contract could fall to around 123.00 over the next few months," said a bond strategist at a European securities company in Tokyo.
Key June JGB futures ended Thursday's Tokyo session up 0.37 at 125.40.
The main bearish factors for JGBs are a firming economy, a weaker yen and stronger stocks, the strategist said.

"The only bullish factor is that the trend of U.S. Treasuries seems to be getting better. If you get a strong rally in Treasuries, that may save JGBs. If not, it would be difficult to be positive on JGBs," he said.
Other analysts also see JGBs heading lower in the medium term.

"June futures look comfortable above 125.00 for now. But any consolidation around this level is unlikely to last more than a week or so. The key contract is more likely to edge down over the medium term," said Ichiro Yamaguchi, a technical analyst at Sakura Securities Co Ltd.
"Tokyo stocks have been quite strong over the last few days. Stock prices are likely to have a significant impact on the direction of JGBs," he added.

Tokyo's Nikkei 225 stock average added another 124.21 points, or 0.65 percent, on Thursday, closing at 19,275.33. It rose as high as 19,588.36 at one point, its highest intraday level since December 24.
Weakness in Tokyo stocks had been one of the major driving forces behind the JGB rally over the past few months.
Analysts see stronger stock prices giving the Bank of Japan (BOJ) greater flexibility in setting monetary policy.

"No near-term rise in Japan's official discount rate is expected. However, more people are realising that ultra-low interest rates will not last forever," said Shunji Sakami, a strategist at LTCB Securities' investment strategy department.

Sakami said most market participants had assumed that the BOJ would maintain its low interest rate policy to help banks tackle the problem of non-performing loans. This view, however, is gradually changing, he said.
"The investment performance of some life insurers and pension funds is deteriorating as interest rates remain stuck at a low level. This problem has been drawing attention recently," Sakami said.
The problem was highlighted last week after the Ministry of Finance (MOF) ordered Nissan Mutual Life Insurance Co to halt some of its operations.
A negative interest rate spread resulting from low interest rates had been cited by some observers as responsible for the medium-sized life insurer's low investment returns.
In addition to the stock market's strength, the yen's weakness is also expected to weigh on JGBs, analysts said.
The dollar rose as high as 127.45 yen on late Thursday in Tokyo, its highest level since August 1992.

"If the dollar continues to rise, it could again put the spotlight on the interest rate gap between the U.S. and Japan, increasing the possibility of an interest rate rise in Japan," said LTCB Securities' Sakami.
The June JGB futures contract set an all-time high of 127.34 on April 8, but the sharp correction that started last Friday pushed the key contract as low as 124.69 on Wednesday.
-- Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-3432-9780
